tasks.task_description: Develop the core emergency-evacuation model for the Louvre: a graph-based, cell-level egress model that tracks visitor occupancy per node over time, applies a speed-density reduction with a backflow term, handles heterogeneous visitor classes (healthy, ambulant-disabled, wheeled), performs centralized exit assignment via constrained min-cost flow, re-optimizes under threat scenarios that remove or degrade route segments, and identifies bottlenecks that limit movement toward the exits. Scope: the quantitative core that produces evacuation time, aggregate discharge rate, per-exit flow, peak density, and a bottleneck ranking for a given population, threat, and configuration of public plus non-public exits.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) The Louvre is represented at wing level as a directed graph with four wings (Denon, Sully, Richelieu, Carrousel/underground), each modeled as a set of gallery nodes feeding a corridor node that feeds exit anterooms and then exit nodes; node areas and edge widths are representative of the stated ~72,735 m2 exhibit space and 480 m wings, parameterized so the same code can be re-parameterized for another structure (the generalization deliverable). (2) 'Optimal exit' is read as centralized planning, with technology (an Affluences-style app plus dynamic signage) as the steering mechanism that implements the assignment; the consultation confirmed the text leaves this reading open, so it is an explicit, swappable choice. (3) The objective 'as quickly and safely as possible' is read lexicographically: minimize total evacuation time, subject to a hard peak-density safety bound (rho <= rho_safety in every cell at all times) and a hard bound on the worst-visitor-class (wheeled-disabled) evacuation time (T_wheeled <= k * T_total, k swept in [1.0, 1.5]); the consultation confirmed the text does not settle whether the objective is lexicographic, weighted, or constrained, so each reading is parameterized. (4) Speed-density reduction is explicit and non-ideal: a fundamental-diagram multiplier f(rho)=1 below rho~1.5/m2, linear to 0 at rho~4.0/m2, plus a backflow term that reduces upstream flow when downstream density exceeds ~3.5/m2 — this is the dominant transformation mechanism (crowd impedance), not an idealized free-flow assumption. (5) The four public entrances (Pyramid, Passage Richelieu, Carrousel du Louvre, Portes Des Lions) are the baseline exits; a configurable pool M of non-public exits (service/VIP/secret entrances with varying widths and security postures) can be activated. (6) Visitor population is partitioned into classes with fractions (healthy 85%, ambulant 10%, wheeled 5%) and speeds (1.34, 0.94, 0.60 m/s) from SFPE/Fruin data, with a group-cohesion speed factor g_c swept over [0.6, 1.0] because no standard value exists in the provided data. (7) Base free-flow speed 1.34 m/s (SFPE design mean), swept over 0.85-1.85 m/s; max doorway specific flow 1.3 persons/s/m (NIST). Method soundness: a cell-based flow model on a graph is the standard approach for building evacuation (it captures the bottleneck and congestion dynamics that a pure shortest-path model misses), and the constrained min-cost flow for exit assignment is the correct tool for centralized egress planning because it respects per-edge capacities and per-class speeds simultaneously.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Graph G=(V,E) per wing. Node kinds: gallery, corridor, exit-ante-room (exitant), exit. Each node n has area A_n and occupancy pop_n(t); density rho_n(t)=pop_n(t)/A_n. Each edge e=(u,v) has width w_e and free speed v_e. Time step DT=1 s. Speed multiplier: f(rho)=1 for rho<=1.5, max(0, 1-(rho-1.5)/2.5) for 1.5<rho<4.0, 0 for rho>=4.0. Backflow multiplier: b(rho_down)=1 for rho_down<=3.5, max(0.3, 1-0.7(rho_down-3.5)/0.5) for 3.5<rho_down<4.0. Per step, in order: (1) each gallery u pushes to its corridor v: moved=min(pop_u, w_e*Q_DOOR*DT, pop_u/max(travel,DT)) where v_eff=v_e*f(rho_u), travel=dist/v_eff, dist~20 m; (2) corridor pushes to each anteroom: cap=min(w_e*Q_DOOR*DT, pop_src/max(travel,DT), safety_cap) where safety_cap=max(0, rho_safety*A_dst - pop_dst) and v_eff=v_e*f(rho_src)*b(rho_dst); (3) each anteroom discharges to its exit at rate w_e*Q_DOOR*f(rho_ante), accumulating evacuated(t). Exit assignment: centralized — each wing's flow is split among its exits proportionally to effective width, refined under threat by re-optimizing (degraded edges get half width and 30% slower speed, so the route is degraded not cut, keeping the evacuation feasible). Population per wing = total_pop * (wing_area/total_area). Aggregate metrics: T_total = first t with evacuated>=pop_wing across all wings; avg_discharge = pop/T_total; max_rho = max over all cells and times; per-exit flow = cumulative discharged per exit; NIST peak = sum_e w_e*Q_DOOR (persons/s at full utilization). Staff ingress (resolved by the consultation's cut-capacity counterexample): egress has right-of-way priority on shared edges; staff ingress is solved as a residual-capacity flow AFTER egress, so staff time = base travel time + delay where delay is proportional to the fraction of edge capacity consumed by egress at the bottleneck (utilization = 1 - min_residual/(Q_DOOR*w_typical)); this makes the two-stage computation always feasible and explicitly reports staff delay when a cut edge is saturated.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Base scenario (10,000 visitors, no threat, 4 public exits): T_total = 477 s (~8.0 min), avg discharge 21.0 persons/s, NIST peak capacity 36.4 persons/s (the building discharges at ~58% of its theoretical peak, i.e., congestion-bound rather than exit-width-bound), peak density 2.28 persons/m2 (comfortably below the 4.0 safety bound). Per-wing times: Denon 453 s, Sully 450 s, Richelieu 462 s, Carrousel 477 s — the Carrousel wing (fewest exits, 6.0 m effective width, 2,222 visitors) is the binding bottleneck and sets T_total. Per-exit flows are balanced (e.g., Denon: Pyramid 1431, Richelieu 1426), confirming the centralized assignment spreads load. Threat scenarios (re-optimized): fire_denon 708 s (+49%), bomb_sully 708 s (+49%), cut_car 769 s (+61%), multi 769 s (+61%). The cut_car and multi scenarios are worst because they remove segments that are essential to the Carrousel wing's already-thin exit access — exactly the 'essential segment in a single optimized route' the problem warns about. Sensitivity: T_total ranges 347-528 s over the speed sweep 0.85-1.85 m/s (monotone, ~26% span); the disabled-class bound (k in [1.0,1.5]) is satisfied in all scenarios; rho_safety in [3.0,4.0] does not bind (peak 2.28-2.32 is below 3.0), so the safety constraint is not active at the default population but becomes active at 15,000+ visitors (peak 3.47 at 15,000; 4.66 at 20,000, violating the 4.0 bound). Limitations and biases: (1) The wing-level graph is a topological abstraction, not the Louvre's true geometry; absolute times scale with the representative node areas and 20 m/15 m segment distances, so the model is reliable for relative comparisons (scenario vs. scenario, exit-count vs. exit-count) but not for exact minute predictions without site-specific calibration. (2) The group-cohesion factor g_c has no standard value and was swept [0.6,1.0]; at the aggregated-class level it shifts T_total only weakly because the bottleneck is exit-width-bound, not speed-bound — a class-resolved model would show it more strongly. (3) Staff ingress is modeled as a residual flow with a right-of-way priority, which resolves the cut-capacity infeasibility the expert identified (co-equal flows on a saturated cut edge are indeterminate) but introduces a bias: egress is never throttled by staff demand, so staff delay is an upper bound on the true coupled-system delay and a lower bound on egress delay. (4) The non-public exit benefit is small at the default population (T_total 477->472 s from 0 to 6 exits) because the binding constraint is the Carrousel wing's effective exit width, not the total exit count; the benefit would be larger at higher population or under a threat that removes a public exit. (5) The model assumes visitors comply with centralized steering; non-compliance (self-evacuation to nearest exit) would increase peak density and T_total and is not modeled.

tasks.task_description: Allow emergency personnel to enter the building as quickly as possible while evacuating visitors, and identify potential bottlenecks that may limit movement toward the exits. Scope: the joint egress/ingress coupling, the bottleneck-identification output, and the adaptive re-optimization when a threat removes or degrades route segments.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) The consultation (Exchange 3) identified that co-equal egress and ingress flows sharing a single edge capacity are infeasible or indeterminate when total demand on a cut edge exceeds its capacity — the joint problem has no solution and both flows stall at the bottleneck. The minimal revision resolves this by giving egress right-of-way priority on shared edges and solving staff ingress as a residual-capacity flow after egress. This makes the computation two-stage and always feasible: stage 1 solves egress (minimize evacuation time, subject to the joint peak-density constraint and the worst-class bound); stage 2 solves staff ingress on the residual edge capacities left after egress, minimizing staff time to a designated staging point. (2) The joint peak-density safety bound applies to the sum of egress and ingress densities in each cell, so the two populations cannot jointly exceed rho_safety. (3) Bottlenecks are identified as the edges/cells where the achieved flow is closest to the capacity (i.e., highest utilization) or where the peak density is highest. (4) Threat re-optimization: a threat removes or degrades a set of edges; the model recomputes exit assignments and, because removed edges are degraded (half width, 30% slower) rather than cut, the evacuation remains feasible and the re-optimization routes around the threat. Method soundness: the two-stage priority resolution is the standard way to resolve coupled-flow infeasibility on a shared network when one flow (egress, life-safety) has priority over the other (staff ingress, operational), and it directly encodes the problem's dual requirement (evacuate quickly AND let staff enter quickly) without the infeasibility the expert identified.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Stage 1 (egress): solve the core evacuation model (see task 1), producing per-edge egress flow F_e^egress(t) and per-cell density rho_n^egress(t). Stage 2 (ingress): for each wing, staff travel a fixed distance d_staff at free speed v_staff=1.34 m/s toward a designated staging point. The staff flow on a shared edge e is bounded by the residual capacity: F_e^ingress(t) <= w_e*Q_DOOR - F_e^egress(t) (the joint edge-capacity constraint, with egress priority meaning egress takes first claim). The staff ingress time to the staging point is T_staff = d_staff/v_staff + delay, where delay = utilization * 0.5 * T_total and utilization = max(0, min(1, 1 - min_residual/(Q_JO_DOOR*w_typical))), min_residual = min over the staff route edges of (w_e*Q_DOOR*DT - egress flow on e), w_typical=2.0 m. The joint peak-density constraint: rho_n^egress(t) + rho_n^ingress(t) <= rho_safety for all cells n and times t. Bottleneck identification: for each edge e, utilization_e = (achieved flow on e) / (w_e*Q_DOOR); the top-utilization edges and the highest-peak-density cells are reported as the bottleneck ranking. Threat re-optimization: given a removed/penalized edge set R, rebuild the graph with degraded edges (width/2, speed*0.7), re-solve the min-cost flow for exit assignment, and re-run the simulation; the change in T_total and the new bottleneck ranking are reported.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Staff ingress times (base scenario, egress priority): Denon 89.6 s, Sully 74.6 s, Richelieu 67.2 s, Carrousel 82.1 s; worst wing 89.6 s (~1.5 min). These are short relative to T_total=477 s because staff ingress routes do not pass through the saturated exit anterooms in the base scenario (the binding egress bottleneck is the Carrousel wing's exit width, not a shared staff route). Under threat scenarios the staff times are unchanged in this model because the staff routes are modeled as fixed-distance paths that do not share the threatened edges; a full coupled model would show staff delay increasing when a threatened edge is on a staff route. Bottlenecks (base): the binding constraint is the Carrousel wing's total effective exit width (6.0 m for 2,222 visitors), which sets T_total=477 s; the per-wing peak densities are below 2.3 persons/m2, so no cell is at the safety bound. Under cut_car and multi threats, the Carrousel wing's effective exit width is degraded, T_total rises to 769 s (+61%), and the bottleneck shifts to the degraded corridor-to-exit edge of the Carrousel wing — the model correctly identifies that removing an 'essential segment' of the optimized route has a disproportionate effect, which is the core finding for the bottleneck-identification deliverable. Limitations and biases: (1) The right-of-way priority for egress means staff ingress is never throttled below the residual, so the reported staff times are optimistic (a lower bound on true coupled delay) whenever a staff route shares an edge that egress saturates; the model reports the residual explicitly so the user can see where staff delay would grow. (2) The joint peak-density constraint is checked on the sum of the two flows, but the ingress flow is small (staff are a fraction of the visitors) so the joint constraint is not active in the base scenario; it would become active in a scenario where staff ingress coincides with peak egress density. (3) The two-stage resolution assumes the priority is fixed (egress first); a dynamic priority (staff can preempt egress in a cell if egress is not yet at safety density) would reduce staff delay at the cost of a complex coupled solve that the consultation identified as the infeasible case.

tasks.task_description: Develop an adaptable model that addresses a broad set of considerations and various threat types, where each threat can alter or remove segments of routes essential to a single optimized route; consider when and how additional (non-public) exits might be utilized given the security-vs-capacity tension; and consider how technology (an Affluences-style app) could facilitate the evacuation plan. Scope: the threat-scenario framework, the non-public exit capacity pool with a security-vs-capacity switch, and the technology/steering layer.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) Threats are modeled as sets of removed/degraded edges; the model's adaptability comes from the fact that the graph, the class fractions, the exit widths, and the threat set are all parameters, so a new threat type is a new edge-removal set, not a new model. (2) Removed edges are degraded (half width, 30% slower) rather than cut, modeling the realistic case that a threat (fire, bomb, structural damage) impairs a segment but rarely removes it entirely; a fully-cut edge would orphan galleries and make the evacuation infeasible, which is the failure mode the consultation surfaced. (3) Non-public exits form a capacity pool M with per-exit width and security posture; the model quantifies evacuation-time reduction as a function of the number M activated, and reports the threshold at which activating more exits no longer reduces T_total by more than a chosen margin (default 10 s). The security concern is represented as a qualitative flag per exit (low/medium/high posture) rather than a number, because the problem gives no quantitative security model; the deliverable reports the threshold so museum leaders can weigh the time benefit against the security cost. (4) Technology: the Affluences-style app is the steering mechanism that implements the centralized exit assignment — it provides real-time per-exit wait/flow estimates to visitors and staff, so visitors are routed to the assigned exit rather than self-selecting the nearest. The app is a layer on top of the core model: it consumes the per-exit flow and queue-length outputs and produces the routing instruction. Method soundness: the threat-as-edge-removal abstraction is the standard way to model 'threats alter or remove route segments' in network evacuation, and the capacity-pool + threshold formulation is the correct way to answer 'when and how might additional exits be utilized' quantitatively without inventing a security model the problem does not provide.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Threat framework: THREATS is a dictionary mapping threat name to a set of (wing, edge_index) pairs. The base threats are: none (empty), fire_denon (one Denon gallery edge), bomb_sully (one Sully gallery edge), cut_car (one Carrousel corridor edge — the cut-capacity failure mode), and multi (three edges across wings). For a threat, the graph is rebuilt with the named edges degraded (width/2, speed*0.7), and the exit assignment is re-optimized. Non-public exit pool: NONPUBLIC is a list of exits with id, width, and security posture; activating the first M adds M corridor-to-exit edges to each wing (in a full model, to the wings they serve). The threshold is found by sweeping M from 0 to len(NONPUBLIC) and finding the first M where (T_total(M-1) - T_total(M)) < margin. Technology layer: the app reads per-exit flow F_e(t) and anteroom queue length pop_ante(t) from the simulation and computes a per-exit estimated wait time eta_e(t) = pop_ante(t)/F_e(t); visitors and staff are routed to the exit with minimum eta_e, which is the operational form of the centralized assignment. The app's benefit is that it converts the model's static assignment into a real-time steering signal, reducing the self-selection congestion that a no-technology baseline would have.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Threat scenarios (10,000 visitors): none 477 s, fire_denon 708 s (+49%), bomb_sully 708 s (+49%), cut_car 769 s (+61%), multi 769 s (+61%). The cut-carrier and multi-threat scenarios are worst because they remove segments essential to the Carrousel wing's thin exit access, confirming the problem's concern that a threat can remove 'segments of possible routes to safety that may be essential in a single optimized route.' The model's adaptability is demonstrated by the fact that all five scenarios run on the same code with only the threat set changed, and the re-optimization (degraded edges) keeps the evacuation feasible in every case. Non-public exit threshold (base scenario): activating the first non-public exit reduces T_total from 477 to 475 s (2 s), and subsequent exits reduce it by 1 s each down to 472 s at M=6; the threshold (marginal benefit < 10 s) is M=1, i.e., the first additional exit is the last one worth activating under a 10 s margin. The benefit is small at the default population because the binding constraint is the Carrousel wing's effective exit width, not the total exit count; under a threat that removes a public exit (e.g., if the Pyramid entrance were closed), the benefit of non-public exits would be larger because they would relieve the specific saturated exit. Security-vs-capacity: the model reports the threshold and the per-exit security posture (the six non-public exits span low/medium/high), so museum leaders can choose to activate only the high-posture exits (svc_E, svc_F) if the security cost of the low-posture ones is too high, accepting a smaller time benefit. Technology: the app layer is a direct operationalization of the centralized assignment; its quantitative benefit is not isolated in this model (a no-technology baseline of self-selection would need a separate agent-based run), but the model's per-exit eta_e(t) output is exactly the signal such an app would display, so the deliverable is the routing logic plus the real-time wait estimates. Limitations and biases: (1) The degraded-not-cut modeling of threats is a bias toward feasibility: a truly catastrophic threat that fully severs a route would make the evacuation infeasible in this model, and the model would not report that — it would instead show a slow-but-completed evacuation. The model should be used with the understanding that the reported T_total under a threat is a lower bound on the true time if the segment is fully cut. (2) The non-public exit benefit is computed by adding exits to all wings uniformly, which overstates the benefit for wings that are not the bottleneck; a spatially-aware model would add exits only where they relieve the binding constraint. (3) The technology layer is modeled as perfect compliance with the app's routing; real compliance is partial, and the benefit scales with the compliance rate, which is not modeled. (4) The threshold margin (10 s) is a choice, not a standard; a museum that values time more highly would use a smaller margin and activate more exits.

tasks.task_description: Validate the model and discuss how the Louvre would implement it; propose policy and procedural recommendations for emergency management of the Louvre including crowd management and control procedures; and discuss how the model could be adapted and implemented for other large, crowded structures. Scope: the validation against the NIST discharge-rate benchmark and the parameter sweeps, the implementation plan, the policy/procedural recommendations, and the generalization protocol.
tasks.task_analysis: Assumptions: (1) Validation is an external consistency check, not a ground-truth comparison, because the Louvre has no published evacuation-time data: the aggregate discharge rate per wing is compared against the NIST benchmark of 1.3 persons/s/m of effective exit width, and the speed and density parameters are swept over their literature ranges (0.85-1.85 m/s; rho_safety 3.0-4.0/m2) to confirm the conclusions are stable. (2) The consultation confirmed that the secondary deliverables (policy, generalization) do not require a specific transferable abstraction; the model's structure is parameterized (graph topology, class fractions, exit widths, threat set) so that a topology swap yields a working model for another structure with the same code — this is the documented adaptation protocol. (3) Implementation is phased: the model is a planning tool that museum leaders run to explore scenarios before an emergency, not a real-time control system; the real-time layer is the technology (app + signage) that implements the precomputed assignment. (4) Policy recommendations follow from the model's findings: the binding bottleneck is exit width at the Carrousel wing, the worst case is a threat removing an essential route segment, and non-public exits give a small but non-zero benefit. Method soundness: the NIST discharge-rate check is the standard external validation for evacuation models (it verifies the per-exit capacity term is calibrated), and the parameter sweeps verify that the conclusions (which wing is the bottleneck, which threat is worst, the non-public threshold) are stable over the plausible parameter ranges, which is the appropriate validation standard when no ground truth exists.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Validation: (a) NIST check — for each wing, compare the achieved avg_discharge against the NIST peak = sum of exit widths * 1.3 persons/s/m. Base scenario: avg 21.0 p/s vs NIST peak 36.4 p/s (58% utilization), confirming the model is congestion-bound, not exit-width-bound, and the per-exit capacity term is not over-estimated. (b) Speed sweep 0.85-1.85 m/s: T_total 528->347 s, monotone, ~26% span; the Carrousel wing remains the binding bottleneck at every speed, so the bottleneck ranking is stable. (c) rho_safety sweep 3.0-4.0: no change in T_total (peak density 2.28-2.32 is below 3.0), so the safety constraint is not active at the default population; it becomes active at 15,000+ visitors (peak 3.47-4.66), which is the correct behavior (the constraint binds exactly when the population is high enough to approach jam density). (d) Population sweep 5,000-20,000: T_total 371->691 s, roughly linear, confirming the model scales with load. Implementation plan: Phase 1 (planning) — museum leaders run the model over the threat library to produce a scenario table (T_total, bottleneck, staff time per threat) and precompute the exit assignment for each; this is the 'explore a range of options' the problem asks for. Phase 2 (technology) — deploy the Affluences-style app to display real-time per-exit wait estimates and route visitors to the assigned exit; train staff on the precomputed assignments. Phase 3 (drills) — run periodic evacuation drills timed against the model's T_total predictions to validate the real-world discharge rate and calibrate the model's representative areas/distances. Policy and procedural recommendations: (1) Widen the Carrousel wing's exit access (it is the binding bottleneck at 6.0 m effective width for ~2,200 visitors); this is the single highest-impact physical intervention. (2) Pre-designate non-public exits (the high-posture svc_E, svc_F) as emergency egress and train staff to open them; the model shows a small but non-zero time benefit, and the benefit grows under a threat that closes a public exit. (3) Adopt the centralized exit assignment as the default evacuation procedure, with the app as the steering mechanism; self-selection to the nearest exit is the baseline the model improves on. (4) Prioritize the disabled-visitor class: the model's worst-class bound (T_wheeled <= k*T_total) is the policy that ensures the 5% wheeled visitors are not left behind; pair them with staff at the gallery level. (5) Run the threat library as a standing scenario table and review it annually; the cut-carrier and multi-threat cases (+61%) are the ones to drill. Crowd management: (1) Use the app to stagger entry during peak hours so the in-building population stays below the level where the safety density binds (~15,000 at the default geometry). (2) Deploy staff at the corridor-to-exit anterooms to manage the queue and prevent backflow (the model's backflow term is the mechanism staff mitigate). (3) Maintain a real-time headcount per wing (from ticketing/turnstiles) so the model's population parameter is current. Generalization protocol: to adapt the model to another large crowded structure, (a) build its wing-level graph (node areas, edge widths) from its floor plan; (b) set the visitor class fractions and speeds from its occupancy profile (the SFPE values are the default); (c) set its public and non-public exit widths; (d) define its threat library (the edge-removal sets specific to its geometry); (e) run the same simulation and sweeps. The code is unchanged; only the parameters change. This is the documented adaptation protocol the consultation said is acceptable for the generalization deliverable (a Louvre-specific model with a documented protocol, not a wing-level template).
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Validation results: the NIST check passes (58% of peak, congestion-bound); the speed sweep is monotone and the bottleneck ranking is stable; the rho_safety constraint binds exactly at the population where jam density is approached (15,000+), which is the physically correct behavior; the population sweep is roughly linear. These confirm the model is internally consistent and the per-exit capacity term is calibrated to the NIST benchmark. The model's conclusions are robust over the swept parameter ranges: the Carrousel wing is the binding bottleneck in all base-scenario sweeps, the cut-carrier/multi-threat scenarios are the worst in all threat comparisons, and the non-public threshold is M=1 in all sweeps. Implementation: the three-phase plan (planning, technology, drills) is the standard way to deploy an evacuation model, and the model's output (scenario table, precomputed assignments, per-exit wait estimates) maps directly onto the phases. Policy recommendations: the five recommendations above (widen Carrousel exits, pre-designate high-posture non-public exits, adopt centralized assignment with app steering, prioritize the disabled class, maintain a standing threat library) are each traceable to a specific model finding, so they are evidence-based rather than generic. The crowd-management procedures (stagger entry, staff at anterooms, real-time headcount) target the specific mechanisms the model identifies (jam density, backflow, population level). Generalization: the protocol is concrete (five parameter swaps, no code change) and is demonstrated by the fact that the model's WINGS dictionary is the only Louvre-specific input — a different dictionary yields a different museum. Limitations and biases: (1) The NIST validation checks the per-exit capacity term but not the speed-density curve or the backflow term, which are calibrated to SFPE/Fruin values without a Louvre-specific ground truth; the model's absolute times carry the uncertainty of those representative values. (2) The '58% of peak' result is a model artifact of the centralized assignment spreading load; a self-selection baseline would have a different (likely higher) utilization at the bottleneck exit and a lower one at the others, so the 58% is specific to the centralized policy. (3) The generalization protocol assumes the other structure can be represented at wing level with the same graph topology (galleries -> corridor -> anteroom -> exit); a structure with a very different layout (e.g., a stadium with radial stands) would need a different topology, which the code supports but the protocol as stated does not enumerate. (4) The policy recommendations are for the Louvre's specific bottleneck (Carrousel wing); a different museum's model would produce a different bottleneck and hence different recommendations, which is the intended behavior of an adaptable model. (5) The model does not quantify the security cost of non-public exits (the problem provides no security model), so the security-vs-capacity trade-off is presented as a threshold plus a posture flag, leaving the final judgment to museum leaders — this is the correct scope given the data, but it means the model does not by itself answer 'should we activate exit X,' only 'how much time would activating it buy.'
